source.title: An Information Theory of Compute-Optimal Size Scaling, Emergence, and Plateaus in Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops a theoretical graph and information-theoretic framework to derive a compute-optimal size/data allocation, rather than measuring loss scaling in trained language models.
record.gate_note: The paper's own compute-optimal allocation result and numerical optimization are recorded for V3. Its discussion of other scaling and emergence work is background. The empirical points attributed to Hoffmann et al. are cited results, not this study's results. The excess-entropy lower bound is recorded as a related finding, not as a test of held-out loss power laws.
record.test_reason: The study is purely theoretical. It trains and measures no language model. Its equal N/D scaling comes from maximising the expected number of 'concepts learnt' in an abstract concept-text bipartite graph under 6ND ≤ C, using LDPC finite-length analysis. V3 concerns the held-out-loss-minimising split of real trained language models, so this objective and subject are a different construct. The result is a model-based explanation of the Chinchilla rule, not evidence on whether the rule holds, and is recorded under fits_no_version. Figure 3(a) compares against the Chinchilla point (5.76e23 FLOPs) cited from Hoffmann et al., which is a cited result. Figure 3(b) compares a derived lower bound with empirical excess entropy cited from Hoffmann et al.; the study has no loss data of its own. If one instead treats the derivation as a T2 test of V3, the verdict could only be supports within the abstract framework, with no empirical bearing.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. More precisely, the authors claim their LDPC/random-graph framework derives the Chinchilla equal-scaling rule as provably optimal, rather than assuming it. They say it explains emergence as a giant-connected-component phase transition in skill graphs, and plateaus as a consequence of multimodal skill-level demands. They predict that plateaus signal further emergences with more scaling. They note the framework ignores training time, so double descent and grokking are out of scope.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a theoretical concept-text graph, peeling process, and LDPC finite-length analysis; it does not reproduce the original empirical training and loss-fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis depends on its graph-model assumptions, including model size being proportional to the number of learnable concepts and a single-epoch concept-peeling process. The numerical example specifies ς = 2 × 10^5, τ = 8 × 10^5, and dt = 6.

fits_no_version.finding: In a concept-text bipartite graph model with peeling (LDPC-erasure) learning, maximising expected learned concepts under 6ND ≤ C gives R/T asymptotically constant, i.e. N and D scale equally with C (Proposition 1; Fig. 3a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abstract skill/concept-graph models of learning can reproduce Chinchilla-style equal compute-optimal scaling without assuming it.

fits_no_version.finding: The framework yields a size-dependent lower bound on excess entropy (Eq. 8) that lies below the empirical curve cited from Hoffmann et al. (Fig. 3b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Graph-based concept-learning theory gives a lower bound on excess-entropy scaling consistent with empirical curves.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Journal on Selected Topics in Signal Processing
record.problems: The compute-optimal result is theoretical and depends on abstract graph assumptions; the numerical size-allocation curves are presented graphically, and no trained-model loss measurements validate the derived allocation.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were left out.

untested.parts: No measured loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; only a theoretical lower bound plotted against a cited curve.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No empirical loss-minimising allocation; only an abstract concept-learning objective is optimised.
No other modalities or training regimes.
The emergence and plateau accuracy curves are model-generated illustrations with chosen parameters, not measured downstream performance.
No comparison of fitting choices or of published laws.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V3 'supports' label is downgraded. Nothing in the study measures a language model, and the optimised quantity (concepts learnt) is not loss. The emergence and plateau results (Fig. 4) come from hand-chosen parameters (L=100, ηl=exp(7l/L), etc.) and are illustrative, not data. Peer-review status is uncertain: the text is labelled 'Preprint. Under review'.

versions.untested_parts: No measurement of held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or tests of predictions on much larger runs.

The allocation is derived within an abstract graph model by maximizing learned concepts, not by measuring held-out loss on trained runs. No numerical scaling exponents or empirical loss-minimizing split are reported.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture choices.
No tests in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream task performance measurements or predictions from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across parameter-counting conventions, schedules, datasets, or fitting methods.

rows.subject: proposed graph-based language-model framework
rows.operation_detail: Theoretically optimize the number of learned concepts under a compute-budget constraint, then derive the asymptotic scaling of the optimal model and dataset sizes.

conditions.value: concept-text bipartite graph with peeling-based concept learning
maximize expected number of learned concepts

rows.measure: Compute-optimal model size N and dataset size D scaling with compute C
rows.value: N and D must scale equally with increasing compute budget C.
rows.note: This is a theoretical result for the framework's learned-concept objective, not an empirical loss-minimization result.
rows.check: Subject is an abstract graph model and the measure is expected concepts learnt, not held-out loss of trained language models, so the row does not measure what V3 names. Proposition 1 only shows R/T is asymptotically neither o(1) nor ω(1); it gives no exponent. The proof also says 'minimizes' where 'maximizes' is meant.

rows.subject: proposed graph-based language-model framework
rows.operation_detail: Numerically solve the constrained optimization for compute-optimal model and dataset sizes across compute budgets.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal model size N* and dataset size D* versus FLOPs C
rows.note: The text says the curves are parallel on a logarithmic scale. Markers are identified as empirical predictions from Hoffmann et al.; those cited values are not this study's results.
rows.check: Numerical optimisation within the same abstract model, with chosen ς=2e5, τ=8e5, dt=6. The parallel log-log curves are not a loss-minimising allocation of trained models. The Chinchilla markers are cited, not measured.

rows.subject: proposed graph-based language-model framework
rows.operation_detail: Derive a lower bound on excess entropy from the framework's training-error estimate and compare its plotted size dependence with empirically observed scaling cited from prior work.
rows.measure: Lower bound on excess entropy as a function of model size
rows.note: This concerns excess entropy and a theoretical lower bound; it does not establish a held-out-loss power law.
rows.check: Theoretical lower bound on excess entropy; the 'empirical' curve is cited from Hoffmann et al. No held-out loss is measured, so it cannot bear on V1.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
